content.p: For several days in late September 1906, white mobs moved through downtown Atlanta and attacked Black residents. They pulled people from streetcars, beat them in the street and destroyed Black-owned businesses and homes. The violence began after Atlanta newspapers printed reports of four assaults on local white women. None of those reports was ever substantiated. The official count was 12 Black residents and two white people killed, but other counts run much higher, and sources still disagree about how many Black residents died.
content.h2: A city of new money and old fears
content.p: By the early 1900s Atlanta had become the commercial hub of the region, and it was growing fast. The New Georgia Encyclopedia reports that the city's population rose from 89,000 in 1900 to 150,000 in 1910. The Black population had grown from about 9,000 in 1880 to 35,000 by 1900. Competition for jobs between Black and white workers grew, and the city's white leaders had responded by widening Jim Crow segregation in neighborhoods and on public transport.

The growth of a Black middle class was also a source of friction. Black-owned businesses were competing with white ones in the Peachtree Street area, and many white residents resented their success. Historian Clarissa Myrick-Harris of Morehouse College told HISTORY that white business owners "didn't like that" competition, and she described a wider fear of Black rule.

The 1906 Democratic race for governor made race the central issue. Hoke Smith, the former publisher of the Atlanta Journal, argued that Black men had to be disenfranchised so that they would be kept "in their place." Clark Howell, editor of the Atlanta Constitution, said the white primary and the poll tax already limited Black voting, and he attacked Smith for having once worked with Black political leaders. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says Smith had the public backing of former Populist Thomas E. Watson.

The newspapers went further. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says papers including the Atlanta Georgian and the Atlanta News ran stories through the year about alleged assaults on white women by Black men, along with editorials and cartoons about a rising crime wave. HISTORY reports that the Atlanta Georgian ran a three-part series on the "reign of terror" against seven white women, and quotes Myrick-Harris saying that in a couple of cases the women said the attacks had not happened to them. Historians therefore describe the reports as unsubstantiated and sensational. The National Center for Civil and Human Rights brief says a play based on Thomas Dixon's novel The Clansman opened in Atlanta in the winter of 1906 and romanticized the Ku Klux Klan; the story became the film The Birth of a Nation in 1915.

On the afternoon of Saturday 22 September, Atlanta papers reported four alleged assaults on local white women. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says the papers issued a series of extra editions that day with more lurid details, and that thousands of white men and boys gathered downtown in protest. Mayor James G. Woodward tried to calm the crowds and failed.

By early evening the crowd had become a mob. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says it surged down Decatur Street, Pryor Street and Central Avenue and through the central business district until after midnight, attacking hundreds of Black people. The mob smashed the windows of the barbershop owned by Alonzo Herndon, who was at home at the time, and raided another barbershop across the street, where the barbers were killed. NPR's report, citing a family account, says that the crowd reached Peachtree Street near Herndon's barbershop, where 13-year-old Walter White saw a boy with a withered foot clubbed to death. White's memoir, excerpted by The Black Commentator, calls the victim a lame bootblack from that barbershop.

The mob also attacked the streetcars. Its members entered the trolleys and assaulted Black men and women. The militia was summoned around midnight, and streetcar service was suspended, but the crowd did not stop. It broke up only when a heavy rain began around 2 a.m., according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia.
content.h2: Sunday and Monday: vigilantes and Brownsville
content.p: On Sunday 23 September the newspapers reported that the state militia had been mustered and that Black residents had been driven off the public streets. Black Atlantans did not trust that calm. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says that Black residents obtained weapons secretly, and that white vigilante groups still entered some Black neighborhoods. In some places residents defended their homes and turned the attackers back. The New York Times reports that some Black residents also fired on attackers, while white groups moved into Black neighborhoods looking for more people to attack.

On Monday 24 September, a group of Black residents met in Brownsville, a community about two miles south of downtown and home to Clark College and Gammon Theological Seminary. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says the attendees were carrying weapons. Fulton County police, hearing of the gathering, expected a counterattack and moved into the neighborhood. A shootout followed, and a county police officer was killed. The New York Times names the officer as James Heard. Three militia companies then moved into Brownsville, took weapons from residents and made more than 250 arrests of Black men. Fighting continued sporadically through that day, according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia.

The death toll is the least settled part of the story, and the figures depend on who is counting. NPR reports that the official count was 12 Black residents and two white people killed, and that many historians say dozens of people were murdered. The Atlanta History Center says the violence left 25 Black Atlantans dead, with hundreds wounded and many Black businesses and homes destroyed. HISTORY says the killings claimed at least 25 African Americans and two white residents. The New York Times says at least two dozen Black people were killed and scores more injured.

HISTORY reports that the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition had learned the names of 14 people killed and was trying to identify 11 more, and that its liaison, Allison Bantimba, estimated that up to 100 African Americans may have died. The Black Commentator, a 2006 publication, said at least ten Black people were killed over five days, and that white mobs killed dozens of Black people in all. The New York Times reports that later accounts blamed the rioting for the deaths of two white people. One was a pregnant woman whose heart gave out after she watched two Black men being shot to death.

The sources also differ on dates. The New Georgia Encyclopedia dates the killings to 24 through 26 September, while the New York Times and HISTORY date the start of the violence to the night of 22 September, so the dates also differ by source.

The New Georgia Encyclopedia says more than 250 African American men were arrested, and HISTORY reports roughly 250. According to HISTORY, no arrests were reported among the white Atlantans who beat and killed Black residents. HISTORY also says that many of those arrested had only armed themselves to protect their families and neighborhoods, according to Allison Bantimba of the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition. FOX 5 Atlanta, carrying an AP report, says that about 60 of those arrested were convicted. The same article quotes community organizer Ann Hill Bond saying that no white person was held responsible for any of the deaths.

A Fulton County grand jury cited "inflammatory headlines" as a cause of the violence, according to FOX 5 Atlanta. When J. Maxwell Barber, the publisher of the Voice of the Negro, tied those articles to the campaigns for governor, FOX 5 reports that he was driven out of town.

The city's leaders met with a hand-picked group of Black leaders by Tuesday, according to the New York Times. The paper says this began a tradition of interracial dialogue that became known as "the Atlanta way," and that the group was chosen by the white elite, which, in the view of Myrick-Harris, meant it was not equal. The Atlanta Evening News stopped publishing, and city leaders visited Black churches to promise safeguards against further mob violence, according to HISTORY.
content.h2: Memory, a name and the long fight
content.p: The riot changed the city's politics and its makeup. FOX 5 Atlanta reports that Smith's laws, passed once he was governor, kept most Black people from the polls for roughly fifty years, and that thousands abandoned Atlanta. The National Center for Civil and Human Rights brief puts the number who left at as many as a thousand. FOX 5 adds that the city had become two-thirds white by 1910, the Census showed. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says the riot also contributed to statewide prohibition and Black suffrage restriction by 1908. The New York Times says scores of middle-class Black residents left the city and that segregation grew more entrenched. The Times describes Alonzo Herndon as Atlanta's first Black millionaire; FOX 5 reports that he left barbering and built a large insurance business serving Black families.

The riot also shaped national Black politics. The New York Times reports that it helped spur the formation of the NAACP, and cites the riot as a life-changing experience for Walter White, who later headed the organization. The National Center for Civil and Human Rights brief dates the founding of the NAACP to 1909. NPR reports that W.E.B. Du Bois wrote the poem "The Litany of Atlanta" after the violence, and that the riot helped move Black activists away from the accommodationist approach associated with Booker T. Washington. The New York Times adds that the historian David Fort Godshalk argues the riot disproved Washington's belief that hard work and respectability would earn white protection.

For decades the event was left out of timelines and textbooks. The New York Times, writing for the centennial in 2006, reports that when the communications director of the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historic Site, Saudia Muwwakkil, reached out to community leaders about the centenary, almost none of them had heard of it. Author Mark Bauerlein retells the story in his book Negrophobia, NPR reports. Historians, activists and descendants began a concerted effort around the centenary, with walking tours, memorial services, new books and a state curriculum change. FOX 5 Atlanta reports that the massacre was added to Georgia's eighth-grade curriculum in 2007.

The name remains disputed. Many accounts still use "riot," and some people argue the word is a whitewash because it implies unrest by a minority group, the New York Times reports. Ann Hill Bond, who leads a campaign to change the name, told FOX 5 Atlanta that the events were a massacre and that people were killed. The Atlanta History Center also says "massacre" may be a more apt term than "riot." Events continue each September; Rough Draft Atlanta reports events in 2023 marking the 117th anniversary, including a symposium at Emory School of Law and a documentary on WABE.
